summary: Defines a MIB textual convention for BCP 47 language tags, so other MIB modules can reuse it. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a shared way for network management tools to write down which human language, like English or French, a piece of text is in.

questions: mib textual convention for language tags
what is the langtag textual convention
what is the max length of a langtag
subtitle: One shared MIB definition for writing down a BCP 47 language tag, so every MIB module does not reinvent it.

tldr.problem: MIB modules that need to store a language tag each defined their own representation, and the older shared one (LanguageTag from RFC 2932) had an outdated, less complete syntax description.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5131 defines the LangTag textual convention in its own small MIB module: a lowercase-only BCP 47 language tag stored as an octet string of 2 to 63 octets, or empty to mean no tag.
tldr.outcome: New MIB modules should import LangTag instead of LanguageTag. The module defines no managed objects, so it has no security impact of its own.

today: RFC 5131 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It states that it replaces the LanguageTag convention in RFC 2932 for new MIB modules.

sections.title: Why a New Language Tag Type
sections.content:
RFC 5131 defines a textual convention named LangTag that represents a BCP 47 language tag. The intent is that other MIB modules import it, instead of defining their own representation.

It replaces the similar LanguageTag textual convention from RFC 2932, which some existing MIB modules still use. New MIB modules should use LangTag because its syntax description is current and more comprehensive, it is short enough to use as an index object without subtyping, and it lives in a dedicated MIB module that keeps module dependencies simple.

A new name was needed because changes in syntax and length cannot be applied to an existing textual convention.
sections.plainLanguage: The old label for language names was out of date and could not be fixed in place. So the authors made a new label with a new name, and asked everyone building new things to use it.

sections.title: The Management Framework Context
sections.content:
Managed objects live in a virtual information store called the Management Information Base (MIB), and are usually accessed through the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP). Objects are defined with the Structure of Management Information (SMI).

This memo specifies a module that is compliant with SMIv2, described in RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580. For the wider picture of the Internet-Standard Management Framework, it points to section 7 of RFC 3410.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of a big shared filing cabinet that network tools use to read and set facts about devices. This document adds one new type of label to the cabinet's rulebook.

sections.title: The LangTag Definition
sections.content:
The module is named LANGTAG-TC-MIB. Its LangTag type has the display hint 1a, status current, and the syntax OCTET STRING (SIZE (0 | 2..63)).

  • Only lowercase characters are allowed, so that tags are unique when used as indexes. BCP 47 recommends case conventions for user interfaces, but objects using this type MUST use only lowercase.
  • Values MUST be well-formed language tags as defined in BCP 47. An implementation MAY limit itself further to what a validating processor accepts.
  • BCP 47 tags are in theory of unlimited length. This type is limited, and the text says the analysis of tag lengths in BCP 47 confirms the limit will not pose a problem in practice.
  • A zero-length value is not a valid language tag. It can be used to express that a language tag is absent, for example in an index field.
sections.plainLanguage: The label must be written in small letters only, so that two spellings of the same language do not look like two different languages. An empty label means no language is given.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The module defines no management objects. It defines only a textual convention that other MIB modules may import and use in their own object definitions.

The RFC states that meaningful security considerations can only be written in the MIB modules that define management objects. It therefore concludes that this document has no impact on the security of the Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: This document is only a label, not a thing you can poke at, so there is nothing here to attack. Any safety rules belong to the tools that use the label.

sections.title: IANA Assignment
sections.content: LANGTAG-TC-MIB is rooted under the mib-2 subtree. IANA assigned { mib-2 165 } to the module. The module identity is named langTagTcMIB, and its first and only revision is dated 9 November 2007.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA is like the registry office. It gave this new module its own spot, number 165, in the big numbered list of management modules.
